title: Kali leaves Nala
hookLine: Damayanti sends out a question, and on the road to her, Kali finally lets Nala go
carry: hearing a sacred story is a shelter
last: SATYA, TRUTH, HAS A POWER OF ITS OWN.

lines: HE DOESN'T WANT TO BE FOUND.
cards: How do you find someone who doesn't want to be found? Damayanti's husband lost everything at dice, walked into the forest with her, cut their one shared cloth while she slept, and left.
She survived the forest and made her way home to her father's house in Vidarbha, to her children. Nala is out there somewhere, changed, hidden, ashamed. A king's daughter could send riders.
Damayanti sends something smaller and sharper. And on the road back to her, something finally lets him go.

teach.b: She calls Brahmanas, travelers who go from court to court, and gives them a question to repeat wherever people gather.
In paraphrase: where have you gone, gambler, after cutting half the cloth of the wife who loved you and leaving her asleep in the forest? Have mercy, and answer.
In a far city, a plain charioteer answers it, and Damayanti knows.
So she sets a trap made of love: word goes out that she'll choose a husband again tomorrow, so soon that only Nala's driving could bring a king there in time.
On that wild drive, King Rituparna teaches his charioteer the secret of dice, and the moment Nala knows it, Kali comes out of him. Not the goddess Kali; a different name.

teach.h: ON THE ROAD, KALI LEAVES HIM
teach.b: This Kali is the spirit of strife, and the same word names the dark age, Kali Yuga. He had slipped into Nala through one small lapse, and it was with Kali inside him that Nala gambled away his kingdom and left his wife.

teach.h: TELL HIS STORY, AND DON'T FEAR ME
teach.b: Leaving, Kali makes Nala a promise: people who tell your story with care won't need to fear me. The whole tale is being told to Yudhishthira in exile, a king who has also just lost everything at dice, to comfort him.
Here's the teaching. Many Hindu texts close with a phala-shruti, the fruit of hearing: a blessing promised to whoever listens. Nala's story carries one in Kali's own mouth.

teach.h: HEARING A SACRED STORY IS A SHELTER.
teach.b: A sacred story isn't only a record; hearing it is a kind of shelter. Some Hindu families still read Nala's story in a bad stretch of life, and in parts of South India it's tied to hard times under the planet Shani.
Back in Vidarbha, Damayanti sends their children to the charioteer, and watches him weep.

how: Hindus know Damayanti's search from the Mahabharata's forest book, where Brihadashva tells it to the exiled Yudhishthira; it is also retold in later poems, plays and dance.

she sent Brahmanas with a question only he would understand.
Kali in this story is the goddess Kali

games.q: you're Yudhishthira, in exile after losing everything at dice. a sage offers you a story. why might he choose Nala's?
o: to prove that dice are always cursed.
a king lost it all at dice and was found again, and the story itself keeps Kali away.
to pass a long night in the forest.
games.why: Brihadashva tells it to comfort him, and the story carries Kali's own promise: those who tell it needn't fear him.

practice: If you're in a hard stretch, name it to yourself in one plain line. Then, the way families read Nala's story in bad times, tell yourself the shape of his: everything lost, hidden, ashamed, and still searched for and found.
Hold that shape beside yours for a few breaths. If you pray, you can ask for strife to leave your house.

wordCard.voice: Damayanti. The wife who searched with a question only her husband could answer, while on the road to her, Kali let him go.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the princess of Vidarbha in the Mahabharata's story of Nala.

carryVoice: Your line: hearing a sacred story is a shelter. Kali promised to spare whoever tells Nala's. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana (Damayanti sends Brahmanas with her question; the charioteer's answer; the second swayamvara announced; Rituparna teaches Nala the science of dice on the drive; Kali leaves Nala and promises that those who tell Nala's story will not fear him; the children sent to him; the frame: Brihadashva tells the tale to Yudhishthira in exile)
